topics.kicker: Temple to Athena atop the Acropolis · Icon of ancient Greek art
topics.briefing: High above Athens, builders raised a dazzling marble temple without a single truly straight line — its platform curves upward and its columns bulge just enough to trick the eye into seeing perfect symmetry. Pericles ordered it built for Athena, and the sculptor Phidias filled it with carvings so prized that arguments over who should own them continue today.

tossups.p: Architects Ictinus [“ik-TY-nus”] and Callicrates [“kuh-LICK-ruh-teez”] designed this building atop a sacred hill, replacing an unfinished predecessor the Persians had destroyed in 480 BCE. Construction, which lasted from 447 to 432 BCE, was partly funded using treasury money diverted from the Delian League.
tossups.r: This Doric building’s badly weathered metopes once showed Centaurs battling the Lapiths. For 10 points, name this temple to Athena on the Acropolis in Athens.

tossups.p: Before this building stood, an earlier temple on the same spot lay unfinished when the Persians burned it in 480 BCE. Pericles later commissioned a replacement, choosing a design that curves its platform upward by several centimeters and lets its columns bulge slightly, optical-illusion tricks that make every line look perfectly straight.
tossups.r: Its sculptor Phidias also built the gold-and-ivory Statue of Zeus at Olympia. For 10 points, name this temple to Athena atop the Acropolis of Athens.

tossups.p: On this building’s south side, battered carvings once showed the Lapiths and their ally Theseus fighting mythical Centaurs. Fifteen of the ninety-two such panels were pried off in the early 1800s and were headed for a British estate before they ended up in a London museum instead.
tossups.r: The sculptor responsible for them, Phidias, also crafted a towering gold-and-ivory statue of the building’s dedicatee. For 10 points, name this Doric temple on the Acropolis, dedicated to Athena.

tossups.p: A French artist named Jacques Carrey [“kah-RAY”] sketched this building’s sculptures in 1674, which turned out to be a lucky bit of timing. Thirteen years later, a Venetian mortar shell ignited Ottoman gunpowder stored inside, blowing off much of its roof during a siege.
tossups.r: Many of its surviving marble carvings were later shipped to England by the Earl of Elgin and now sit in the British Museum. For 10 points, name this ancient temple atop the Acropolis in Athens.

tossups.p: This building’s columns swell slightly partway up, a refinement called entasis, while its whole platform curves upward about ten centimeters across its length. Both tricks correct optical illusions that would otherwise make its perfectly straight lines look like they sag or curve inward.
tossups.r: A modern city law keeps most of Athens’s buildings under about twelve stories partly so views of this temple stay open. For 10 points, name this Doric temple to Athena on the Acropolis.

tossups.p: A continuous carved band, unusually done in the Ionic style for an otherwise Doric building, wrapped the cella of this structure and depicted an idealized Panathenaic [“pan-ath-uh-NAY-ik”] procession. Phidias oversaw the whole project and also crafted this building’s cult statue.
tossups.r: That nearly forty-foot statue of Athena was made of gold and ivory and held a small figure of Nike in one hand. For 10 points, name this temple on the Acropolis of Athens.

tossups.p: This building’s back room once held the Delian League’s pooled funds, since it doubled as a treasury in addition to its religious role. Pericles pushed for its construction over objections that the money should not be spent beautifying the city.
tossups.r: Ictinus and Callicrates designed this replacement for an unfinished temple the Persians had destroyed. For 10 points, name this temple to Athena atop the Acropolis in Athens.

tossups.p: The name of this structure likely comes from the Greek word “parthenos,” meaning virgin or maiden, since it housed a statue honoring Athena under that same title. Scholars still debate exactly which room or rooms the name originally referred to.
tossups.r: Sculptures removed from this building by the Earl of Elgin remain a major point of dispute between Greece and Britain. For 10 points, name this ancient Greek temple on the Acropolis in Athens.

tossups.p: A full-size concrete replica of this building, complete with a new forty-two-foot statue of Athena by sculptor Alan LeQuire, stands in a park in Nashville, Tennessee. The original building’s own chryselephantine [“kry-suh-LEF-un-teen”] statue of Athena has been lost since ancient times.
tossups.r: That original gold-and-ivory statue was created by the sculptor Phidias. For 10 points, name this temple on the Acropolis of Athens that the Nashville building copies.

tossups.p: Battered metopes on this building’s south face depict a mythical battle between Centaurs and the Lapiths, a people aided by the hero Theseus. On the building’s east end, a now-lost pediment sculpture once showed the birth of this temple’s honoree.
tossups.r: Marble panels from its pediments and frieze are now controversially displayed in London as the Elgin Marbles. For 10 points, name this Doric temple to Athena atop the Acropolis.

tossups.p: Workers curved this building’s foundation and entablature upward by roughly four inches across its length and gave its columns a subtle outward swell, refinements meant to correct how a true rectangle would look slightly concave from a distance.
tossups.r: This building replaced an older temple the Persians destroyed in 480 BCE. For 10 points, name this temple to Athena that Pericles had built on the Acropolis in Athens.

tossups.p: In the early 1800s, agents working for a British diplomat removed roughly half of this building’s surviving sculptural decoration, including metopes, pediment figures, and sections of its frieze. Greece has formally asked Britain to return those marbles since 1983.
tossups.r: Those sculptures are now known as the Elgin Marbles. For 10 points, name this Doric temple on the Acropolis of Athens, from which they were taken.

tossups.p: This building’s sculptor also created a seated, gold-and-ivory statue of Zeus at Olympia, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. Inside this building, that same sculptor’s Athena statue once stood nearly forty feet tall.
tossups.r: Ictinus and Callicrates served as its architects. For 10 points, name this temple to Athena that stands atop the Acropolis in Athens.

tossups.p: Jacques Carrey’s 1674 sketches of this building’s sculptures became invaluable after a 1687 gunpowder blast damaged many of the originals. Centuries later, a full-size replica in Nashville, Tennessee, received a new Athena statue by Alan LeQuire.
tossups.r: This building’s own ancient Athena statue, by the sculptor Phidias, has long since been lost. For 10 points, name this Doric temple on the Acropolis in Athens.

tossups.p: Funded partly with treasury money taken from the Delian League, this building replaced an unfinished temple that Persian forces had destroyed in 480 BCE. Its name likely derives from “parthenos,” an epithet of its honoree meaning virgin or maiden.
tossups.r: Pericles oversaw its construction between 447 and 432 BCE. For 10 points, name this temple dedicated to Athena atop the Acropolis of Athens.

trap.title: Parthenon or Acropolis?
trap.body: The Acropolis is the whole flat-topped hill in Athens, home to several buildings: the Parthenon, the smaller Erechtheion with its six carved maiden columns, the gateway called the Propylaea, and the tiny Temple of Athena Nike. Real tossups about “the Acropolis” often mention the Parthenon as just one clue among several, and some even pause to prompt if a player blurts out “Parthenon” before the word itself is read.
trap.fix: Listen for clues about OTHER buildings too — caryatids or the Porch of the Maidens mean the Erechtheion, a gateway means the Propylaea. If the question only ever describes one specific temple (metopes, a chryselephantine Athena statue, Ictinus and Callicrates), it is safe to answer “Parthenon.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Parthenon. A separate, related answer line, the Acropolis, covers the whole hilltop and may prompt if “Parthenon” is named before it is read.

topics.name: Statue of Liberty
topics.kicker: Colossal statue in New York Harbor · France’s gift of liberty to America
topics.briefing: In 1886, France gave the United States a gift too big to wrap: a copper woman more than fifteen stories tall, holding a torch over New York Harbor. Her sculptor had first dreamed up a giant lighthouse for Egypt’s Suez Canal, and the iron skeleton inside her copper skin was engineered by Gustave Eiffel — years before he built a certain tower in Paris.

tossups.p: This sculpture’s design recycled an earlier, rejected project: a lighthouse called “Egypt Carrying the Light to Asia” that its creator had proposed for the entrance to the Suez Canal at Port Said. An eleven-pointed star fort forms part of its 154-foot pedestal.
tossups.r: A broken chain and shackle lie half-hidden by its robes at its feet. For 10 points, name this colossal statue in New York Harbor, a gift from France.

tossups.p: Gustave Eiffel engineered the iron skeleton inside this statue’s copper skin, years before he built a much taller tower in Paris. French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi designed the statue itself, which was dismantled into crates and reassembled after crossing the Atlantic.
tossups.r: It was dedicated on October 28, 1886. For 10 points, name this statue of a robed woman holding a torch in New York Harbor.

tossups.p: A 1903 bronze plaque at this statue’s base carries a sonnet written twenty years earlier for a fundraising auction, including the line “Give me your tired, your poor.” That poem, Emma Lazarus’s “The New Colossus,” nicknames this statue’s figure “Mother of Exiles.”
tossups.r: The statue’s tablet reads “JULY IV MDCCLXXVI” in Roman numerals. For 10 points, name this statue that has welcomed immigrants to New York Harbor since 1886.

tossups.p: Architect Richard Morris Hunt designed this statue’s granite pedestal, which was partly funded by small donations collected through Joseph Pulitzer’s newspaper, the _New York World_. Over 120,000 people gave money, most of it less than a dollar each.
tossups.r: Sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi had reused an earlier lighthouse design meant for Egypt. For 10 points, name this statue that France gave to the United States in 1886.

tossups.p: This statue’s current torch, installed in a 1986 renovation, is an exact replica of the original covered in 24-karat gold leaf. Its seven crown spikes are popularly said to stand for the seven seas and continents, though historians have not confirmed that symbolism.
tossups.r: Gustave Eiffel engineered its internal iron frame. For 10 points, name this statue that stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor.

tossups.p: Before designing this statue, French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi had proposed a similar giant lighthouse, shaped like a robed peasant woman, for the entrance to the Suez Canal. Egypt’s ruler rejected that design as too costly.
tossups.r: This statue instead became a gift from France honoring the two countries’ alliance during the American Revolution. For 10 points, name this copper statue holding a torch in New York Harbor.

tossups.p: Workers assembled this statue’s copper skin over an iron framework engineered by Gustave Eiffel, who later designed a much taller Paris landmark. From ground level to the tip of its torch, this statue measures about 305 feet.
tossups.r: Its copper surface, now green from oxidation, was originally a shiny brown color. For 10 points, name this statue dedicated in New York Harbor in 1886.

tossups.p: A broken chain and shackle rest at this statue’s feet, half-hidden by its robes, symbolizing freedom from oppression. The statue itself stands 151 feet tall, not counting its pedestal, which rises from the star-shaped walls of an old fort.
tossups.r: Emma Lazarus’s sonnet “The New Colossus” is engraved on a plaque inside its base. For 10 points, name this statue of a woman holding a torch and tablet in New York Harbor.

tossups.p: Before this statue existed, its sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi tried to interest Egypt in a similar lighthouse statue for the Suez Canal. Funds for this statue’s pedestal came partly from pennies and dimes collected by Joseph Pulitzer’s newspaper.
tossups.r: Its tablet reads “JULY IV MDCCLXXVI,” marking American independence in Roman numerals. For 10 points, name this statue France gave the United States, dedicated in 1886.

tossups.p: This statue’s internal iron support structure, engineered by Gustave Eiffel, had to survive being shipped across the Atlantic Ocean in pieces inside more than 200 crates. Its sculptor had first imagined a similar robed figure for the Suez Canal in Egypt.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this statue of a woman holding a torch and a tablet reading “JULY IV MDCCLXXVI,” which stands in New York Harbor.

tossups.p: This statue’s pedestal was designed by architect Richard Morris Hunt and rises from the star-shaped walls of an old fort. The poet Emma Lazarus wrote a sonnet to help raise money for that pedestal, decades before the poem was actually placed inside it.
tossups.r: That sonnet calls this statue’s figure the “Mother of Exiles.” For 10 points, name this statue on Liberty Island, holding a torch over New York Harbor.

tossups.p: This statue’s thin copper skin, no thicker than two pennies stacked together, covers an iron framework strong enough to withstand ocean winds. Sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi had earlier proposed a similar robed figure as a lighthouse for the Suez Canal.
tossups.r: Gustave Eiffel engineered that internal ironwork. For 10 points, name this statue dedicated on October 28, 1886, that France gave to the United States.

tossups.p: A chain lies broken at this statue’s feet, and its crown bears seven spikes often said to represent the seas and continents. Architect Richard Morris Hunt designed the granite pedestal on which it stands, raised partly by Joseph Pulitzer’s newspaper campaign.
tossups.r: This statue’s tablet is inscribed with the date of American independence in Roman numerals. For 10 points, name this statue holding a torch over New York Harbor.

tossups.p: Sculptor Bartholdi recycled the concept for this statue from an unbuilt Egyptian lighthouse. It was planned for the 1876 centennial of American independence, honoring the wartime alliance between the United States and the country that gave it.
tossups.r: Gustave Eiffel designed the iron skeleton that still supports its copper skin today. For 10 points, name this statue in New York Harbor.

tossups.p: Emma Lazarus’s 1883 poem about this statue was not actually placed on a plaque at its base until 1903, seventeen years after the statue’s own dedication. That poem describes this statue’s figure holding “a torch, whose flame is the imprisoned lightning.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this statue in New York Harbor, gift of France, sculpted by Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi.

trap.title: Eiffel, or the Eiffel Tower?
trap.body: Gustave Eiffel engineered the Statue of Liberty’s internal iron frame years before he built his famous tower in Paris. A clue naming “Gustave Eiffel” describes this statue, not the Eiffel Tower itself — a very easy, very common early-buzz mistake.
trap.fix: If the clues mention New York Harbor, a torch, a tablet, or Bartholdi, the answer is the statue. Eiffel only engineered its skeleton; he did not design the statue itself, and the Eiffel Tower is a completely separate French landmark he built later.
trap.line: Real answer line: Statue of Liberty (accept Liberty Enlightening the World)

topics.name: Mona Lisa
topics.kicker: Leonardo da Vinci’s portrait in the Louvre · The world’s most famous smile
topics.briefing: She has been smiling for more than 500 years, and people still cannot agree on why. Around 1503, Leonardo da Vinci began this small portrait using sfumato, a soft, smoky blending technique with no harsh outlines, and may have kept reworking it for over a decade. Stolen from the Louvre in 1911 and parodied by artists ever since, she is now the most famous painting on Earth.

trap.title: The Painting, or the Heist?
trap.body: Some real tossups ask about the famous 1911 theft itself as its own separate answer — “Theft of the Mona Lisa” — packed with clues about Vincenzo Peruggia, Guillaume Apollinaire, and Pablo Picasso being questioned by police. Buzzing “Mona Lisa” on one of those is a wrong, early guess.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This woman,” “this painting,” or “this portrait” means the painting itself. “This crime,” “this theft,” or “this event” means the 1911 heist — a related but separate answer line.

topics.name: Guernica
topics.kicker: Picasso’s anti-war mural · Mourns the bombing of a Basque town
topics.briefing: In 1937, German and Italian warplanes bombed the Basque town of Guernica during the Spanish Civil War, an attack that shocked the world. Pablo Picasso answered with a huge black-and-white mural full of pain and protest: a screaming horse, a raging bull, and a mother grieving over her child, with no uniforms or flags in sight. In 1974, a protester even spray-painted “KILL LIES ALL” across the original while it hung at New York’s Museum of Modern Art.

trap.title: Painting or painter?
trap.body: Quiz bowl always wants the title of the artwork, not its creator. A tossup that says “name this painting” or “name this mural” wants the title, not Pablo Picasso, even though every single clue describes a choice Picasso made. The painting is also sometimes confused with Picasso’s other 1937 response to the same war, _The Weeping Woman_, a related but separate work.
trap.fix: Listen for “painting,” “mural,” or “work” — that always means the title. If the question instead asks “who painted…,” the answer is Picasso, not the title.

topics.name: Mount Rushmore
topics.kicker: Colossal mountain carving in South Dakota · Honors four U.S. presidents
topics.briefing: Between 1927 and 1941, sculptor Gutzon Borglum and a crew of workers carved four 60-foot-tall presidential faces into a South Dakota mountain: George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln. The mountain’s original Lakota name was the Six Grandfathers, and the carving still upsets many Native Americans because the Black Hills are sacred to the Lakota people. Movie heroes have even fled villains across its granite faces, most famously in Alfred Hitchcock’s _North by Northwest_.

trap.title: Mount Rushmore or Crazy Horse?
trap.body: Mount Rushmore and the nearby Crazy Horse Memorial are both giant sculptures carved into mountains in South Dakota’s Black Hills, and quiz bowl writers love to describe one while asking about the other. Crazy Horse honors a single Lakota leader and is still unfinished after being started in 1948 partly in response to Mount Rushmore. Mount Rushmore shows the faces of four presidents and was finished, as far as it ever would be, in 1941.
trap.fix: Listen for the subject. Clues about a lone Native American warrior, an unfinished work, or “the world’s largest sculpture” point to Crazy Horse. Clues about four presidents, Gutzon Borglum, or _North by Northwest_ point to Mount Rushmore.

topics.name: Notre Dame Cathedral
topics.kicker: Gothic cathedral on an island in Paris · Setting of Hugo’s bell-ringer novel
topics.briefing: Started around 1163 on an island in the Seine River, Notre Dame Cathedral took nearly two centuries to finish and became one of the finest examples of French Gothic architecture, famous for its flying buttresses, stone gargoyles, and three glowing rose windows. Victor Hugo set his novel about the bell-ringer Quasimodo inside its towers, and Napoleon crowned himself emperor there in 1804. A devastating fire tore through the cathedral’s roof and spire in 2019, but a major restoration brought it back in 2024.

topics.name: Sistine Chapel
topics.kicker: Vatican chapel · Home to Michelangelo’s ceiling and _The Last Judgment_
topics.briefing: Pope Sixtus IV built this chapel as his own private place of worship in the Vatican — then, decades later, Pope Julius II talked a reluctant sculptor named Michelangelo into painting its ceiling from custom scaffolding, standing and craning his neck back, not lying down as legend claims. The result includes _The Creation of Adam_, where God’s finger almost touches Adam’s, and decades later Michelangelo returned to paint _The Last Judgment_ across the altar wall.

tossups.p: Some art historians think the red cloth and tangled figures surrounding God in one ceiling panel here secretly outline a human brain, an idea a physician proposed in 1990. Painted thrones around that ceiling’s edges hold five Sibyls and seven Hebrew prophets, and one central panel shows Noah embarrassingly drunk after the Flood.
tossups.r: Michelangelo designed his own standing scaffolding to spend roughly four years painting that ceiling for Pope Julius II. For 10 points, name this Vatican room whose altar wall Michelangelo later covered with _The Last Judgment_.

tossups.p: One panel on this room’s ceiling shows a pink-robed figure twice, reaching out to create the sun and the moon on the same day of Genesis. Elsewhere on that ceiling, the same figure’s finger almost brushes the finger of a reclining, newly formed man.
tossups.r: Pope Sixtus IV built this room in the 1470s, but it is best known for the ceiling Michelangelo painted a few decades later. For 10 points, name this Vatican chapel housing _The Creation of Adam_.

tossups.p: After the Council of Trent, a painter nicknamed the “breeches-maker” was hired to add loincloths over nude figures on this room’s altar wall. On that same wall, the ferryman Charon beats condemned souls with an oar while demons drag sinners down toward Hell.
tossups.r: Michelangelo hid a self-portrait on the flayed skin held by Saint Bartholomew in that same mural. For 10 points, name this chapel where Michelangelo painted _The Last Judgment_.

tossups.p: This room’s side walls were painted first, in the 1480s, by Renaissance masters including Botticelli, whose _Punishment of the Rebels_ shows followers of Korah swallowed by the earth. Decades later, Michelangelo reportedly refused the architect Bramante’s scaffold design, which would have left holes through the vault, and built his own instead.
tossups.r: That ceiling took Michelangelo from 1508 to 1512 to finish. For 10 points, name this Vatican chapel, home to Michelangelo’s most famous ceiling frescoes.

tossups.p: A woman many scholars identify as Eve waits tucked beneath God’s left arm in one scene on this room’s ceiling, while God’s right hand reaches toward a reclining man. More than 300 figures crowd that ceiling in all, including ancestors of Christ painted into the lunettes above the windows.
tossups.r: Pope Julius II commissioned Michelangelo to paint the whole thing starting in 1508. For 10 points, name this chapel in Vatican City.

tossups.p: Michelangelo reportedly preferred sculpture and resisted this commission for months before Pope Julius II insisted he take it on. Nine central scenes from Genesis run down the middle of this room’s ceiling, bookended by _The Separation of Light from Darkness_ and _The Drunkenness of Noah_.
tossups.r: Decades later, a different pope asked Michelangelo back to paint _The Last Judgment_ on the altar wall. For 10 points, name this chapel in the Vatican.

tossups.p: Figures wrapped in a red cloth are said by some to trace the outline of a human brain around God in this room’s most famous ceiling panel. That same panel, _The Creation of Adam_, also shows God’s fingertip almost touching a newly made man’s.
tossups.r: Smoke from a chimney above this room tells the world whether cardinals have chosen a new pope. For 10 points, name this Vatican chapel where papal conclaves are held.

tossups.p: Pope Clement VII commissioned a fresco for this room’s altar wall shortly before his death, and Pope Paul III saw it finished in 1541. On the ceiling here, the prophet Jonah leans back dramatically on his painted throne, while sibyls sit on several others nearby.
tossups.r: That altar fresco, _The Last Judgment_, faces scenes Michelangelo had painted on the ceiling decades earlier. For 10 points, name this Vatican chapel.

tossups.p: Before Michelangelo ever touched its ceiling, this room’s side walls were already covered with 1480s frescoes on the lives of Moses and Christ by artists like Perugino and Ghirlandaio. One of those earlier scenes, Botticelli’s _Punishment of the Rebels_, shows Korah’s followers swallowed by the earth.
tossups.r: Decades later, Michelangelo would paint _The Creation of Adam_ on this same room’s ceiling. For 10 points, name this Vatican chapel.

tossups.p: In one ceiling scene here, God appears twice in a pink robe, pointing to form the sun and the moon on the same day of creation. In a much later scene on the altar wall, Charon ferries condemned souls while sinners are dragged down toward Hell.
tossups.r: This room gets its English name from the pope who built it, Sixtus IV, in the 1470s. For 10 points, name this Vatican chapel painted by Michelangelo.

tossups.p: Saint Bartholomew holds his own flayed skin, which many believe hides a self-portrait of the artist, in a fresco on this room’s altar wall. That same artist painted the ceiling here from his own scaffolding, standing and bending backward, for roughly four years.
tossups.r: Tourists now crowd beneath both of Michelangelo’s masterpieces in this single room. For 10 points, name this chapel in Vatican City.

tossups.p: An artist nicknamed “Il Braghettone,” or “the breeches-maker,” was later hired to cover nude figures on this room’s altar wall after the Council of Trent objected to their nudity. On the ceiling nearby, the prophet Jeremiah sits lost in thought on his painted throne.
tossups.r: Both that altar fresco and the ceiling above it were painted by Michelangelo. For 10 points, name this Vatican chapel, home to _The Last Judgment_.

tossups.p: Figures encircling God in red drapery may hide the outline of a human brain, according to one widely discussed theory about a panel on this room’s ceiling. That same panel, admired for centuries, shows God’s finger nearly touching the finger of a man lying on a green hillside.
tossups.r: This chapel’s walls were frescoed decades before its famous ceiling by painters like Botticelli and Perugino. For 10 points, name this Vatican chapel whose ceiling Michelangelo painted.

tossups.p: This room takes its English name from the Italian pope who had it built between 1473 and 1481. Michelangelo returned to this room roughly twenty-five years after finishing its ceiling to paint _The Last Judgment_ on the wall behind its altar.
tossups.r: Cardinals gather in this chapel to elect new popes, burning their ballots in a stove connected to a chimney. For 10 points, name this Vatican chapel.

tossups.p: Nine central panels telling stories from Genesis, from _The Separation of Light from Darkness_ to _The Drunkenness of Noah_, run down the middle of this room’s ceiling. Michelangelo designed his own scaffolding, built on brackets rather than ropes, to paint them all starting in 1508.
tossups.r: He returned to paint _The Last Judgment_ on the altar wall of this same room decades later. For 10 points, name this Vatican chapel whose ceiling Pope Julius II commissioned.

topics.briefing: Edward Hopper painted this diner scene in 1942, just after the attack on Pearl Harbor, when blacked-out windows made American cities feel lonelier than ever. Inside, three customers sit under cold fluorescent light while a white-uniformed counterman works behind the counter — and famously, there is no door for anyone to walk through. It hangs today in the Art Institute of Chicago, one of the most reproduced and parodied paintings in American art.

topics.briefing: Auguste Rodin first planned this bronze figure to crown a sculpted doorway called _The Gates of Hell_, brooding over the souls of Dante’s _Inferno_ far below. Rodin’s assistant later enlarged him to his famous six-foot size, and the hunched, muscular pose came to stand for deep thought everywhere, not just one poet’s nightmare. A cast of this very statue now marks Rodin’s own grave.

topics.briefing: Shah Jahan, the Mughal emperor of India, built the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died giving birth to their fourteenth child. Finished around 1653 after nearly twenty years of work by thousands of artisans, its white marble walls are inlaid with colorful gemstones in floral patterns. Today the Taj Mahal stands in Agra as one of the New Seven Wonders of the World and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

topics.kicker: Dalí’s painting of melting clocks · A Surrealist icon at MoMA
topics.briefing: In 1931, Spanish artist Salvador Dalí painted _The Persistence of Memory_, a dreamlike scene of limp, melting watches draped over a dead tree, a table’s edge, and a strange sleeping face. Dalí later said the soft clocks came to him after watching a wheel of Camembert cheese melt in the sun. Now owned by the Museum of Modern Art in New York, this small canvas remains one of the most recognizable Surrealist paintings ever made.

topics.kicker: Grant Wood’s 1930 farm couple · One of America’s most parodied paintings
topics.briefing: In 1930, Iowa artist Grant Wood painted _American Gothic_, showing a stern farmer gripping a pitchfork beside a woman in front of a small white farmhouse. Wood’s own sister and his dentist posed as the models, and the Gothic-style window on the house gave the painting its name. Now hanging in the Art Institute of Chicago, it has become one of the most recognized and most parodied images in American art.
